Does married filing separately get the auto loan interest deduction?

Yes. Married filing separately (MFS) is not excluded from this deduction.

That surprises a lot of filers, because two other new 2025 deductions this portfolio has calculators for -- the "no tax on tips" / "no tax on overtime" deduction and the senior deduction -- both exclude MFS entirely. The auto loan interest deduction runs the opposite way: each spouse who files separately gets their own independent $10,000 cap.

How an MFS spouse's cap works

Each MFS spouse tests their own modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) against the single-filer thresholds -- not the higher joint thresholds -- and claims the deduction on their own separate return:

ItemMFS (per spouse)Married filing jointly (combined)
Cap before phase-out$10,000, on each spouse's own return$10,000 total, shared by both spouses
Phase-out starts at MAGI$100,000 (each spouse's own MAGI)$200,000 (combined household MAGI)
Fully phased out at MAGI$150,000 (each spouse's own MAGI)$250,000 (combined household MAGI)
Reduction rate$200 per $1,000 (or part) over the thresholdSame $200 per $1,000 (or part) over the threshold

Worked example: same household income, two filing statuses, very different result

Two spouses, Spouse A and Spouse B, each finance their own eligible vehicle and each pay $8,000 of qualifying interest in the year. Their combined household MAGI is $240,000 either way -- only the filing status changes.

ScenarioMAGI testedCap after phase-outDeduction
Spouse A, filing MFS, MAGI $120,000$120,000 vs. single-filer $100k-$150k range$10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000$6,000
Spouse B, filing MFS, MAGI $120,000$120,000 vs. single-filer $100k-$150k range$10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000$6,000
MFS combined household deduction$240,000 combined—$12,000
Same couple, filing jointly, combined MAGI $240,000$240,000 vs. joint $200k-$250k range$10,000 − $8,000 = $2,000 (one shared cap)$2,000

At this specific combined income, filing separately produces a combined deduction six times larger than filing jointly -- because each MFS spouse's MAGI is tested against the lower, single-filer phase-out range independently, rather than the household's full combined MAGI being tested against the higher joint range all at once. Reverse the numbers -- one spouse earning most of the household income -- and the comparison can flip. There is no substitute for running your own numbers both ways.

This is the one sibling calculator where MFS is not shut out

Every other new-2025-deduction calculator in this portfolio treats MFS the same way: excluded entirely. This one does not, and that inconsistency is set by the statute itself, not by any pattern worth assuming holds across deductions:

DeductionMFS treatment
Auto loan interest (this page)Eligible -- own $10,000 cap per spouse
No tax on tips / no tax on overtimeExcluded entirely
Senior deductionExcluded entirely

Common questions

Does married filing separately (MFS) qualify for the auto loan interest deduction?

Yes. Unlike the separate 'no tax on tips' and 'no tax on overtime' deductions, which exclude MFS entirely, the auto loan interest deduction does not exclude MFS. Each spouse who files separately gets their own $10,000 cap on their own return.

What income threshold applies to an MFS return?

The same $100,000-$150,000 MAGI range used for single filers and heads of household -- not the $200,000-$250,000 joint range. Each MFS spouse's own MAGI is tested against the single-filer thresholds independently.

Can filing separately produce a bigger combined deduction than filing jointly?

Yes, in some cases. Two spouses each earning $120,000 MAGI (a combined $240,000) and each paying $8,000 of qualifying interest on their own vehicle loan can deduct $6,000 apiece filing MFS -- $12,000 combined. The same couple filing jointly, at the same $240,000 combined MAGI, shares one cap reduced to $2,000 total for the household -- a sixth of the MFS combined result.

Why is the MFS rule opposite to this portfolio's other 2025 deduction calculators?

Congress wrote each OBBBA deduction with its own filing-status rules; there is no single consistent MFS treatment across them. The 'no tax on tips' and 'no tax on overtime' deductions exclude MFS filers entirely. The senior deduction also excludes MFS. The auto loan interest deduction does not -- it is the one sibling calculator in this portfolio where an MFS filer is not automatically shut out.

Does this mean married couples should always file separately for this deduction?

Not necessarily. Filing status affects your entire return, not just this one deduction -- other credits, deductions, and tax brackets change with it too. This page and its calculator only show the auto loan interest math for each scenario; compare your full return both ways, or ask a qualified tax professional, before choosing a filing status because of this deduction alone.

Run your own numbers

The auto loan interest deduction calculator applies this same cap and phase-out logic to your own MAGI, interest paid, and filing status, and walks through the full eligibility checklist. Nothing you enter is uploaded.

AUTO LOAN INTEREST DEDUCTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's the new car loan interest deduction worth?

A new federal deduction applies to tax years 2025 through 2028: up to $10,000/year of interest paid on a loan for a new, US-assembled, personal-use vehicle — but only if eight eligibility conditions are all met, and it shrinks once your income clears $100,000 (single/HoH/MFS) or $200,000 (joint). This checks every condition and estimates the deduction, including the married-filing-separately rule most people assume works the opposite way it actually does.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status & income

MAGI here is modified adjusted gross income — for most filers with no foreign income or certain exclusions, this is close to the AGI on last year's return, adjusted for this year's income. Married filing separately uses the same $100,000 threshold as a single filer, applied to each spouse's own return.

2. Loan interest

This is the interest portion of your loan payments this year — not your monthly payment and not the vehicle's price. Your lender's year-end statement (Form 1098, where applicable) or loan amortization schedule shows this figure.

3. Eligibility checklist

All eight must be true. If even one is not, none of the interest above qualifies for this deduction — the deduction is not prorated for a partially-eligible vehicle or loan. The cap itself does not double for a joint return even when every item below is met — see the results below and the FAQ.

Fill in filing status, MAGI, and interest paid, confirm the checklist, then click Calculate.

Estimate

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates one deduction only — not your total tax liability, other deductions or credits, or state tax.
  • Eligibility is self-reported — final assembly location, lien status, and vehicle classification are confirmed by you, not verified here. Check the vehicle's window sticker or decode its VIN with NHTSA's VIN decoder before relying on the final-assembly checkbox.
  • Payroll and state tax are unaffected — see the footer disclaimer.
  • Refinanced loans and loans that pay off an earlier vehicle loan have their own rules this calculator does not model — check current IRS guidance if your loan was refinanced.

Common questions

How much car loan interest can I deduct?

Up to $10,000 per year of qualified interest paid on a loan for a new, personal-use passenger vehicle finally assembled in the United States, for tax years 2025 through 2028. This is a deduction on the INTEREST you pay, not the price of the vehicle or the loan amount, and it phases out for higher earners -- see the phase-out question below.

Does the $10,000 cap double for married filing jointly?

No. Unlike some other new deductions, a married couple filing jointly shares ONE $10,000 cap between them, not $10,000 each. Married filing separately works differently -- see the next question.

Can I claim this if I file married filing separately?

Yes -- and this is the detail most people assume is wrong, because this portfolio's own separate 'no tax on tips and overtime' deduction calculator excludes MFS entirely. This auto loan interest deduction does NOT exclude MFS: each spouse gets their own $10,000 cap on their own separate return, phased out using the same $100,000-$150,000 MAGI thresholds a single filer uses.

What is the income phase-out?

The deduction is reduced by $200 for every $1,000 (or part of $1,000) that your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $100,000 (single, head of household, or married filing separately) or $200,000 (married filing jointly). It reaches exactly $0 at $150,000 MAGI (single/HoH/MFS) or $250,000 MAGI (joint).

What vehicles qualify?

A NEW car, minivan, van, SUV, pickup truck, or motorcycle with a gross vehicle weight rating under 14,000 lbs, with final assembly in the United States, bought (not leased) for personal use with a loan secured by a first lien on the vehicle. RVs and campers do not qualify even when used as a primary residence. A salvage-titled vehicle, a vehicle bought for scrap or parts, a fleet purchase, and a vehicle used in a trade or business are all excluded.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published statutory cap, phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to the numbers and checkboxes you enter. It is not a full tax return, it does not verify your vehicle's final assembly location or your loan's terms, and it is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

This calculator vs. doing it by hand

The auto loan interest deduction looks like simple arithmetic — a cap, a phase-out, a checklist. The problem is that two of its rules run opposite to what people assume after reading about a similar 2025 deduction, and a quick by-hand estimate tends to copy the wrong assumption over.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Married filing separatelyAssumes MFS is excluded, generalizing from this portfolio's own tips/overtime deduction (which DOES exclude MFS).Applies MFS eligibility correctly, with its own $10,000 per-spouse cap at the single-filer thresholds, and flags the difference explicitly.
The cap for joint filersAssumes the $10,000 cap doubles to $20,000 for a joint return, the way some other per-filer caps do.Applies the correct single, shared $10,000 cap for a joint return and says so in the results.
Final assembly locationAssumes eligibility from the brand's country of origin rather than checking the specific VIN or window sticker.Asks the question directly as part of an 8-item checklist, rather than assuming an answer.
The MAGI phase-outRounds the excess over the threshold down to the nearest $1,000 instead of up.Reduces the deduction by $200 per $1,000 of MAGI over the threshold, rounding the excess UP ("or fraction thereof").
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake estimating this deduction by hand?

Assuming married filing separately is excluded, because this portfolio's own 'no tax on tips and overtime' deduction excludes MFS and people generalize that rule to every new 2025 deduction. This one does not exclude MFS -- each spouse gets their own $10,000 cap on their own return.

What's the second most common mistake?

Assuming the $10,000 cap doubles for a joint return, the way some other per-filer caps do. It does not -- a married couple filing jointly shares one $10,000 limit between them, not $10,000 each.

What eligibility condition gets missed most often?

Final assembly location. A vehicle being 'made in America' by brand reputation is not the same as its specific VIN showing US final assembly -- many models built by US and foreign brands alike are assembled in Mexico, Canada, or elsewhere, and a by-hand estimate often assumes eligibility from the brand name instead of checking the window sticker or VIN.

What about the MAGI phase-out?

A by-hand estimate often forgets the excess MAGI rounds UP to the next $1,000, not down -- so $100,001 of MAGI already costs the first $200 of the deduction, the same as $100,999 does.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your full return -- other deductions, credits, or state conformity. Both apply the same published federal cap, phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to the numbers you enter; verify against the IRS's own guidance or a qualified tax professional before filing.
